notes: Indecent images appeal; Landslide propensity evidence wrongly deployed and jury misdirected; conviction quashed with no retrial.

enrichment.short_title: R v Simons: Landslide propensity evidence and indecent images on computer
key_facts: Simons was convicted of making and possessing indecent images of children found as thumbnails on his computer hard drive.
Prosecution relied on Landslide database entries from 1999 showing access to child pornography sites using his details, plus adult DVDs with suggestive titles.
The defence said images arrived via spam or Trojan and that someone else used his identity on Landslide.
No objection was taken at trial to admissibility of the Landslide and DVD material.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on admissibility and summing-up grounds relating to Landslide evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed as unsafe; no retrial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Prior access to child pornography sites and propensity evidence may not be deployed solely to show paedophilic interest where it is not relevant to the charged offences; where such material is admitted only to rebut accident it requires careful jury direction, and use as propensity contrary to Makin and Wright vitiates a conviction.
legal_issues: Admissibility of Landslide database evidence as propensity rather than rebutting accidental possession
Whether denial of Landslide access made the evidence relevant to credit
Adequacy of jury directions on the significance of propensity evidence
Safety of conviction where prejudicial material featured prominently in summing-up
linked_authorities: Makin v Attorney General for New South Wales [1894] AC 57
R v Wright (1990) 90 Cr App R 325
R v B(RA) [1997] 2 Cr App R 88

confidence.notes: Admissibility ruling, quashing and refusal of retrial are clearly reasoned in a complete judgment.

notes: Post-ECJ Alabaster maternity pay appeal; Court of Appeal disapplied EPA comparator requirement and allowed ERA time-bar challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Alabaster v Woolwich: statutory maternity pay and Article 141 equal pay remedy

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mrs Alabaster's SMP was calculated on pre-increase earnings for the statutory reference period despite a December 1995 pay rise before maternity leave.
The ECJ held a pay rise between the reference period and end of maternity leave must be included in SMP calculations.
Her ERA unlawful-deduction claim was dismissed as time-barred and she had no male comparator for an EPA claim.
Ten systematic differences between ERA and EPA enforcement regimes disadvantaged maternity pay claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing after ECJ preliminary ruling on whether failure to backdate a pay rise breached Article 141 and whether an effective domestic remedy existed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; EPA comparator requirement disapplied so she could recover £204.53 plus interest; Secretary of State ordered to pay costs including ECJ reference.
enrichment.ratio: Where Article 141 rights to equal pay during maternity leave can only be enforced through the ERA, materially less favourable procedural protections than the EPA regime cannot be objectively justified; the EPA may be applied without a male comparator following Webb.
legal_issues: Whether Article 141 required inclusion of a mid-reference pay rise in SMP
Whether the ERA or EPA provided the effective remedy for breach of EC equal pay rights
Compatibility of shorter ERA time limits and weaker protections with EC principles of equivalence and effectiveness
Whether Article 14 ECHR required equal procedural treatment with other equal pay claimants
linked_authorities: Case C-147/02 Alabaster v Woolwich PLC [2004] ECR
Gillespie v Northern Health and Social Services Board [1996] ICR 499
Webb v EMO Air Cargo (UK) Ltd (No 2) [1995] ICR 1021

confidence.notes: ECJ ruling applied with detailed comparison of statutory remedies and clear final orders.

notes: Libel summary judgment application against solicitors; Tugendhat J refused CPR 24 relief pending privilege waiver and fuller disclosure.

enrichment.short_title: Creative Resins v Glasslam solicitors: libel and qualified privilege at interlocutory stage
key_facts: Creative Resins sued Glasslam and its solicitors over letters to Classic Door Panels alleging copyright infringement, defective laminate and a prior German injunction.
The solicitors had not served a defence; the claimant pleaded malice and recklessness as to falsity of the German proceedings allegation.
The first defendant relied on qualified privilege but not justification; privilege might not extend to irrelevant defamatory allegations.
The first defendant had not waived privilege over instructions leading to the letters.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under CPR Part 24 for summary judgment or strike-out against the solicitor defendants in a libel claim.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment application dismissed; real prospect of success against solicitors remained and further disclosure or privilege waiver might clarify malice.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor is not a mere conduit for client defamation and must exclude irrelevant defamatory matter; at an interlocutory stage where client privilege is unwaived and malice turns on disputed facts, Part 24 is inappropriate despite extensive correspondence.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors shared qualified privilege with their client on a letter before action to a third party
Whether allegations of prior German injunction and manufacturing defects were relevant to the privileged occasion
Whether malice could be inferred from failure to verify serious allegations
Appropriateness of Part 24 before defence, disclosure and witness statements in a libel action
linked_authorities: Swain v Hillman [2001] 1 All ER 91
Horrocks v Lowe [1975] AC 135
Regan v Taylor [2000] EMLR 549

confidence.notes: Interlocutory refusal is clearly reasoned though ultimate merits at trial remain undetermined.

notes: Clydach quadruple murder appeal; solicitor conflict of interest rendered trial unfair; convictions quashed with retrial ordered.

enrichment.short_title: R v Morris: Clydach murders and solicitor conflict of interest
key_facts: David Morris was convicted of murdering four women at Kelvin Road, Clydach in June 1999.
His solicitor David Hutchison had previously represented police suspects Stephen and Ian Stuart Lewis for sixteen months.
The defence strategy avoided directly accusing the Lewises of murder because of a proviso attached to Hutchison's retainer.
Strong prosecution evidence included Morris's gold chain with Amanda Power's blood found at the scene.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder convictions by leave of the full court on conflict of interest and non-disclosure grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed as unfair; fresh indictment and retrial ordered with venue to be fixed by the presiding judge; wasted costs application against Hutchison adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor who previously represented alternative suspects should not act for the accused where the defence must implicate former clients; a conflict pervading trial strategy deprives the defendant of a fair trial and renders convictions unsafe even without proof of specific prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether Hutchison's dual representation created an inescapable conflict of interest
Impact of an undertaking not to suggest Stephen Lewis committed the murders on defence strategy
Fairness of a trial where alternative suspects were not robustly challenged
Appropriate venue and retrial directions after quashing
linked_authorities: R v Togher [2001] 1 Cr App R 33
R v Forbes [2001] 1 AC 473
Condron v United Kingdom [2001] 31 EHRR 1

confidence.notes: Extremely detailed judgment on conflict facts with clear quashing and retrial orders.

notes: Infant murder appeal post-Cannings; conflicting expert evidence held sufficient; conviction upheld with call to reform infanticide law.

enrichment.short_title: Kai-Whitewind: infant murder, expert evidence and Cannings principles
key_facts: Chaha'oh Niyol Kai-Whitewind was convicted of murdering her three-month-old son Bidziil in August 2002.
The trial issue was deliberate killing versus natural or unexplained death; expert pathologists disagreed on smothering.
Post-conviction fresh evidence and Cannings-based arguments were advanced on appeal.
The court noted the mother's inability to admit killing can complicate infanticide defences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction on Cannings unsafe-conviction principles and application to adduce fresh expert evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe despite expert conflict because independent evidence supported the verdict; fresh evidence not admitted.
enrichment.ratio: After Cannings, conviction based on expert opinion alone is unsafe where experts are of equal standing and the science is uncertain; here ample non-expert and contextual evidence justified the jury's verdict and proposed fresh evidence did not undermine safety.
legal_issues: Application of R v Cannings to convictions resting on disputed medical expert evidence
Admissibility and weight of fresh post-conviction expert evidence
Whether three separate infant deaths in family history supported deliberate killing
Need to modernise infanticide law where mothers deny killing
linked_authorities: R v Cannings [2004] EWCA Crim 1
R v Pendleton [2002] 1 WLR 1528
R v Harris [2005] EWCA Crim 1980

confidence.notes: Detailed Cannings analysis and explicit dismissal with policy observations on infanticide reform.

notes: Teacher's firearm appeal; conviction appeal refused but six-month sentence replaced with conditional discharge.

enrichment.short_title: R v Walker: vigilante firearm use after harassment and sentence appeal
key_facts: Mrs Walker, a teacher of good character, fired an air pistol near youths after prolonged harassment including burglaries at her home.
She took an air rifle and pistol into the street intending to frighten boys who denied involvement; police arrived during the incident.
She was convicted of possessing a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence and affray.
Fresh milkman witness statements were refused on appeal against conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence; full court refused leave on conviction but granted leave on sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal refused; sentence appeal allowed; six months' imprisonment replaced with a twelve-month conditional discharge.
enrichment.ratio: Premeditated discharge of a firearm in public normally merits custody under R v Avis, but exceptional mitigation including prolonged victimisation, good character, psychiatric adjustment disorder and low reoffending risk can justify a non-custodial or much shorter sentence.
legal_issues: Whether fresh witness evidence could render convictions unsafe under section 23
Proportionality of custodial sentence for vigilante firearm use
Application of R v Avis to air weapons discharged to intimidate
Relevance of mental health and harassment history to culpability
linked_authorities: R v Avis [1998] 1 Cr App R 420
R v Ollerenshaw [1999] 1 Cr App R(S) 65

confidence.notes: Clear separate dispositions on conviction and sentence with established sentencing authority applied.

notes: Agency welder unfair dismissal appeal; no contract of service with Skyblue despite continuous assignments.

enrichment.short_title: Bunce v Skyblue: employment agency worker and contract of service
key_facts: Mr Bunce, a welder, worked on 142 assignments over 52 weeks via employment agency Skyblue, mostly for Carillion Rail.
His written agreement expressly stated it was a contract for services and imposed no obligation to accept assignments.
Day-to-day control of his work rested with end-user clients, not Skyblue.
The employment tribunal and EAT held he was neither an employee nor self-employed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on whether separate assignment contracts with Skyblue were contracts of employment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no contract of service with Skyblue existed during assignments; unfair dismissal claim could not proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Delegation of client control through a standard agency clause does not give the agency sufficient control for a contract of service; without mutuality of obligation and day-to-day control by the agency, an agency worker on rolling assignments is not an employee for ERA purposes.
legal_issues: Whether each accepted assignment created a separate contract of service with the agency
Whether clause delegating client supervision satisfied the control test
Application of Dacas and Ready Mixed Concrete criteria to long-term agency placements
Status of full-time agency workers lacking unfair dismissal protection
linked_authorities: Dacas v Brook Street Bureau UK Ltd [2004] IRLR 125
Ready Mixed Concrete (South East) Ltd v Minister of Pensions [1968] 2 QB 497
Montgomery v Johnson Underwood Ltd [2001] ICR 819

confidence.notes: Authoritative application of post-Dacas agency worker principles with clear dismissal.

notes: Bladed article case stated appeal; bail hostel forecourt held not a public place; directed acquittal.

enrichment.short_title: Harriot v DPP: bladed articles and public place at bail hostel
key_facts: Mr Harriot lived at a bail hostel and, after discovering a burglary, put kitchen knives in his pockets.
He was searched in the open forecourt after an angry scene in reception and locked out of the building.
He said he was looking for the offender; magistrates convicted him of possessing bladed articles in a public place.
The forecourt was set back from the road with an ungated gap in a low wall but no evidence of tolerated public access.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative Court appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' convictions under section 139.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted with direction to acquit; costs ordered from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: An ostensibly private front area of a bail hostel is not a public place under section 139(7) merely because access from the highway is unimpeded; public access requires evidence that members of the public use the land as such, not simply that they are not excluded.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'public place' in section 139(7) Criminal Justice Act 1988
Whether ungated access from a highway converts private hostel grounds into a public place
Distinction between lawful visitors and the public generally
Consistency of public place definition across different statutory contexts
linked_authorities: Knox v Anderton [1982] 76 Cr App R 156
Williams v DPP [1992] 95 Cr App R 415
R v Roberts [2003] EWCA Crim 2753

confidence.notes: Clear case stated facts with unanimous appellate reasoning and directed acquittal.

notes: Provisional liquidation creditor list application; rule 12.17 unavailable but section 135(4) function ordered with undertakings.

enrichment.short_title: Equitas v UIC provisional liquidators: creditor list in long-running provisional liquidation
key_facts: UIC Insurance Company had been in provisional liquidation since a 1996 winding-up petition with no winding-up order made.
Equitas, representing about 40% of scheme creditors, sought names of the top 50 creditors in value.
Rule 12.17 did not apply because no winding-up order had been made despite deemed commencement arguments.
Many creditors preferred confidentiality but class rights on a winding-up petition justified limited disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application under Insolvency Rules rule 7.2 for an order requiring provisional liquidators to furnish a creditor list.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted under section 135(4); provisional liquidators ordered to provide top 50 creditor names to Equitas subject to use undertakings and ICC confidentiality limits.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 12.17 requires an actual winding-up order and cannot be invoked during a prolonged provisional liquidation; section 135(4) empowers the court to confer a function of distributing creditor names where a class right is invoked and no statement of affairs exists.
legal_issues: Whether rule 12.17 applied without a winding-up order
Construction of section 129(2) deemed commencement of winding up
Use of section 135(4) to require provisional liquidators to disclose creditor information
Appropriate undertakings to prevent misuse of creditor names

notes: Operation Mink covert surveillance appeal; deliberate bugging of solicitor-client yard talks made prosecution abusive; conviction quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Grant v R: covert police surveillance and legal professional privilege
key_facts: Grant was convicted of conspiracy to murder Ian Dowling, his wife's lover, after a Lincoln Crown Court trial.
Lincolnshire police bugged Sleaford police station exercise yards in Operations Wheel, Mink and Galaxy.
Privileged solicitor-client conversations in the yard were recorded in Mink; Astill J refused a stay but Wheel and Galaxy proceedings were stopped.
DS Bennett and other officers were linked across all three operations with inconsistent accounts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on abuse of process following a three-week voir dire; grounds included deliberate eavesdropping and co-defendant cut-throat defence fairness.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on grounds 1 and 3; conviction quashed as unsafe due to abuse of process; grounds 4 and 5 refused.
enrichment.ratio: Deliberate police interception of detained suspects' privileged consultations with solicitors so undermines the rule of law that proceedings are abusive and must be stayed even without evidentiary prejudice; Astill J's contrary finding in Operation Mink could not stand against Wheel and Galaxy findings.
legal_issues: Whether Operation Mink devices were installed to capture solicitor-client communications
Whether prejudice is required to stay proceedings for privilege violations
Effect of Newman J and HHJ Heath findings on parallel Lincolnshire operations
Fairness of co-defendants' late 'team 2' theory in closing speeches
linked_authorities: R v Derby Magistrates Court ex p B [1996] AC 487
R v Horseferry Road Magistrates Court ex p Bennett [1994] 1 AC 42
Brennan v United Kingdom (2001) 34 EHRR 20

confidence.notes: Long judgment synthesising three related operations with clear abuse-of-process conclusion.
